items.stem: A teacher receives an email from "do-not-reply@g00gle.com" asking them to click a link to approve a student's document-access request. Which detail is the strongest indicator that this message is a phishing attempt?

choices.A: The email mentions a student by relationship rather than by name
choices.B: The sender domain "g00gle.com" substitutes zeros for the letter O in "google"
choices.C: The email was sent during school hours
choices.D: The subject line uses an exclamation point

items.explanation: A lookalike domain that swaps characters to imitate a trusted brand (typosquatting) is one of the most reliable technical indicators of phishing, since legitimate organizations don't send mail from spoofed domains.

rationale.A: Vague references to a "student" without a name are a soft social-engineering cue but far less definitive than a forged domain.
rationale.C: Timing alone says nothing about legitimacy; plenty of real institutional email arrives during school hours.
rationale.D: Urgent punctuation is a manipulation tactic, not a technical indicator, students often overweight tone and underweight the sender address.

items.stem: An attacker calls an employee, claims to be from the IT helpdesk, and references the employee's manager by name before asking for a password reset. Which social engineering tactic is this?

choices.A: Pretexting
choices.B: Tailgating
choices.C: Baiting
choices.D: Phishing

items.explanation: Pretexting involves inventing a fabricated scenario or identity, here, a fake IT role bolstered by real-sounding detail, to build false trust and extract information over a direct interaction such as a phone call.

rationale.B: Tailgating is physically following someone through a secured door, not a phone-based ruse.
rationale.C: Baiting lures victims with an enticing physical or digital item (like a USB drive), not an invented identity.
rationale.D: Phishing specifically refers to deceptive messages, typically email, rather than a live phone impersonation.

items.stem: A worker badges into a secure office building, holding the door open for a person carrying boxes who has no visible ID badge. What social engineering risk does this scenario illustrate?

choices.A: Quid pro quo
choices.B: Vishing
choices.C: Whaling
choices.D: Tailgating

items.explanation: Tailgating (or piggybacking) is gaining unauthorized physical access by following an authorized person through a secured entry point, exploiting politeness rather than a technical flaw.

rationale.A: Quid pro quo involves offering a service in exchange for information or access, not simply following someone through a door.
rationale.B: Vishing is voice-based phishing over phone calls, unrelated to physical entry.
rationale.C: Whaling is phishing targeted specifically at senior executives, not a building-access scenario.

items.stem: In the phishing email scenario, the message states: "Research shows that the faster teachers respond to students' document-sharing requests, the more likely students are to submit assignments on time." Why does this sentence make the email more persuasive?

choices.A: It explains the technical steps required to share a document
choices.B: It proves the sender is affiliated with an educational research organization
choices.C: It cites a believable-sounding justification that pressures the teacher to act quickly without verifying the request
choices.D: It confirms the student's identity to the teacher

items.explanation: This sentence manufactures false urgency by framing inaction as harmful to students, exploiting the teacher's sense of responsibility to short-circuit careful verification, a classic influence tactic in social engineering.

rationale.A: The sentence is about urgency and consequence, not instructions.
rationale.B: An unverified claim in an email proves nothing about the sender's actual affiliation; that's exactly the point of the manipulation.
rationale.D: Nothing in that sentence identifies any specific student; it speaks only in generalities.

items.stem: An attacker leaves a USB drive labeled "Q4 Salary Review, Confidential" in an office break room. Why is this tactic likely to succeed in getting an employee to plug it in?

choices.A: It requires the employee to enter a password before the attack works
choices.B: It directly exploits a software vulnerability without any user action
choices.C: It relies on the employee already trusting the attacker personally
choices.D: It exploits curiosity and the perceived value of confidential information to override caution

items.explanation: Baiting works by dangling something the target wants, here, sensitive salary information, so curiosity or self-interest overrides normal caution about unknown devices.

rationale.A: No password entry is needed for a USB-based baiting attack to execute.
rationale.B: Baiting requires the victim to take an action (plugging in the drive); it isn't an automatic exploit.
rationale.C: Baiting works precisely because it doesn't require any prior relationship with the attacker.

items.stem: If the teacher in the scenario had clicked the link and entered their school login credentials on the resulting page, what is the most likely organizational impact?

choices.A: The teacher's device is permanently disconnected from the network
choices.B: The school's email server automatically resets all passwords
choices.C: The attacker gains access to the teacher's account and any systems or data it can reach
choices.D: No impact occurs unless the teacher also opens an attachment

items.explanation: Credential harvesting through a fake login page gives the attacker working credentials, enabling account takeover and lateral access to whatever data, email, or shared systems that account can reach, the central impact social engineering attacks are designed to produce.

rationale.A: Compromise typically grants access rather than cutting off connectivity.
rationale.B: There is no automatic system-wide reset triggered by an individual phishing click.
rationale.D: Credential theft itself is the harmful action; no separate attachment is required for the impact described.

items.stem: A school IT administrator is documenting the phishing incident with the teacher's email for a post-incident report. Which combination of evidence most strongly supports classifying this as a targeted phishing attempt rather than generic spam?

choices.A: The email contained no links and only requested a reply
choices.B: The email was sent to one teacher and used formal language
choices.C: The email used a spoofed lookalike domain, referenced a plausible school workflow (document sharing), and created urgency tied to student outcomes
choices.D: The email was flagged by the spam filter before the teacher saw it

items.explanation: Targeted phishing is distinguished from generic spam by the convergence of multiple deliberate elements: domain spoofing for credibility, a pretext relevant to the victim's actual role and context, and engineered urgency, together these show intentional tailoring rather than a mass, indiscriminate blast.

rationale.A: Absence of a link doesn't indicate targeting and is in fact inconsistent with this scenario, which centers on a malicious link.
rationale.B: Single-recipient delivery and formal tone alone are weak signals; both legitimate and generic spam emails can share these traits.
rationale.D: Being caught by a spam filter says nothing about how targeted the message was, it's an outcome of delivery, not evidence of intent.

items.stem: A security awareness trainer is choosing which influence principle to emphasize when teaching staff to resist pretexting calls that impersonate IT support and reference real employee names. Which principle should be prioritized, and why?

choices.A: Scarcity, the call implies a limited-time offer the target doesn't want to miss
choices.B: Authority, attackers borrow the credibility of a trusted role (IT) combined with insider-sounding detail to suppress the target's instinct to verify
choices.C: Liking, the attacker spends time building a personal friendship before asking for anything
choices.D: Social proof, the attacker claims many other employees have already complied

items.explanation: Impersonating IT support exploits authority bias: people are conditioned to comply with requests from perceived organizational power or technical expertise, and pairing that with accurate insider details (a manager's name) further suppresses the instinct to independently verify the caller's identity.

rationale.A: Scarcity relies on urgency around limited availability, which isn't the mechanism described in an IT-impersonation pretext.
rationale.C: Pretexting calls are typically brief and transactional, not built on cultivated rapport over time.
rationale.D: No claim about other employees' behavior is present in this scenario; the leverage comes from role authority, not peer comparison.

items.stem: A district is updating its incident-response checklist after several tailgating and pretexting incidents. Which checklist addition would most directly reduce risk across both attack types, given that they exploit different channels (physical vs. verbal)?

choices.A: A monthly password rotation policy
choices.B: A stronger spam filter on the email gateway
choices.C: Mandatory multi-factor authentication on all cloud accounts
choices.D: A policy requiring independent verification of any unscheduled request for access or information, regardless of how it arrives

items.explanation: Tailgating and pretexting both exploit human trust and the absence of verification rather than a technical weakness, so the common mitigation that addresses both is a verification-first culture, confirming identity or authorization independently before granting physical access or information, regardless of the channel the request comes through.

rationale.A: Password rotation is unrelated to either physical access control or verbal social engineering and doesn't address the root behavioral vulnerability.
rationale.B: Spam filtering only addresses email-based threats and does nothing for in-person tailgating or phone-based pretexting.
rationale.C: MFA protects account logins specifically; it doesn't stop someone from following an employee through a physical door or verbally extracting information.

items.stem: A company wants receiving mail servers to reject any message that shows the company's domain in the visible From: line but fails sender authentication for that domain. Which DNS-published control does this?

choices.A: An SPF record on its own
choices.B: A DKIM public-key record
choices.C: A DMARC record with the policy p=reject
choices.D: An MX record

items.explanation: DMARC ties the results of SPF and DKIM to the domain in the visible From: line (alignment) and tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails: nothing (p=none), send it to spam (p=quarantine), or refuse it (p=reject). It is the only one of the four that both checks the address the reader actually sees and states an enforcement policy.

rationale.A: SPF lists the servers allowed to send for a domain, but it checks only the envelope sender (MAIL FROM), not the From: line the reader sees, and it does not on its own tell receivers to reject anything.
rationale.B: A DKIM record publishes the public key used to verify a message's signature; by itself it does not link the signature to the visible From: domain or tell receivers to refuse unsigned mail.
rationale.D: An MX record only says which servers accept mail for a domain; it plays no part in checking who sent a message.

items.stem: An employee is tricked into typing their password and second-factor code into a convincing fake login page that passes everything to the real site in real time. Which kind of multi-factor authentication would still have kept the attacker out?

choices.A: A FIDO2/WebAuthn security key or passkey registered to the real site's domain
choices.B: A six-digit code from an authenticator app
choices.C: A one-time code sent by text message
choices.D: Security questions about the employee's first school

items.explanation: A FIDO2/WebAuthn key is bound to the exact domain it was registered with. On a lookalike domain the browser reports the wrong origin and the key refuses to sign the login challenge, so there is nothing for the fake page to capture and replay. This origin binding is why NIST counts these authenticators as phishing-resistant.

rationale.B: An authenticator-app code can be typed into the fake page and replayed to the real site within its 30-second window, which is exactly what happened in the 2020 Twitter attack.
rationale.C: An SMS code is relayed the same way as an app code and is also open to SIM-swap attacks, so it is weaker still.
rationale.D: Security questions are something the user knows, the same factor as a password, and the answers are typed straight into the fake page.

items.stem: A finance clerk receives an email from a long-standing supplier asking that next week's payment go to a new bank account "because of an urgent audit." Which control is the recommended response?

choices.A: Reply to the email and ask the supplier to confirm the new account
choices.B: Check that the email carries a valid DKIM signature, then make the change
choices.C: Forward the email to a colleague and ask whether it looks genuine
choices.D: Call the supplier on a phone number taken from the company's own records, not from the email, before changing anything

items.explanation: Out-of-band verification, confirming the request through a separate channel whose contact details you looked up yourself, is the control the FBI's IC3 recommends for any change to payment instructions. It works even when the email really comes from the supplier's mailbox because an attacker has taken it over.

rationale.A: A reply goes back to whoever controls that mailbox; if the attacker has it, the attacker simply confirms.
rationale.B: A taken-over mailbox at the real supplier signs its mail with the supplier's genuine key, so the DKIM check passes and proves nothing about the request.
rationale.C: A colleague reading the same email has no better evidence than the clerk; in the 2016 DNC case a staffer's quick verdict on a phishing email was exactly what let it through.

items.stem: An email's headers show the envelope sender MAIL FROM: billing@cheap-mailer.net with SPF passing for cheap-mailer.net, while the visible From: line reads "Jane Doe, CEO" <jane.doe@victim-corporation.com>. Why did SPF not catch this, and which control closes the gap?

choices.A: The SPF record for cheap-mailer.net is too loose; making it stricter would stop the message
choices.B: SPF checks only the envelope sender, which really was cheap-mailer.net; a DMARC policy on victim-corporation.com requires the authenticated domain to match the visible From: domain
choices.C: SPF only works on encrypted connections; requiring STARTTLS between mail servers would stop the message
choices.D: SPF checks the message body rather than the headers; adding DKIM would make it check the From: line instead

items.explanation: SPF answers one question: is this server allowed to send for the envelope domain? Here it was, because the attacker controls cheap-mailer.net. The reader, however, sees the RFC 5322 From: line, which SPF never looks at. DMARC closes the gap by requiring that SPF or DKIM pass for a domain aligned with that visible From: domain; mail claiming to be from victim-corporation.com without that alignment is then quarantined or rejected.

rationale.A: The attacker writes the SPF record for their own domain, so making it stricter is up to them; SPF passing for cheap-mailer.net is correct behaviour, and the problem is which domain was checked.
rationale.C: STARTTLS encrypts mail in transit but says nothing about who may send as a domain; the spoofed message in the chapter's SMTP transcript was itself sent over TLS.
rationale.D: SPF does not read the body; it compares the sending server's IP address with the envelope domain's list. DKIM signs the message, but on its own it does not require the signing domain to match the From: line.

items.stem: In the July 2020 Twitter incident, the targeted employees had one-time-password MFA, yet the attackers still signed in to internal admin tools. What explains this, and which change would have stopped it?

choices.A: The codes were too short; longer one-time codes would have prevented reuse
choices.B: The employees had switched MFA off; enforcing MFA for everyone would have stopped it
choices.C: The fake VPN portal collected each code as it was typed and replayed it to the real site before it expired; origin-bound FIDO2 keys would have refused to sign for the fake domain
choices.D: The attackers had broken the one-time-password algorithm; switching to SMS codes would have stopped it

items.explanation: The lookalike portal acted as a real-time proxy: it took the username, password and current code and used them on the real site within the code's short validity window. A one-time code proves only that someone has it now, not where it is being typed. FIDO2/WebAuthn keys sign a challenge bound to the genuine domain, so a proxy on a different domain receives nothing it can use.

rationale.A: Code length is irrelevant when the victim hands over a valid code; a longer code is relayed just as easily.
rationale.B: MFA was in use; the attack worked around it rather than finding it switched off.
rationale.D: Nothing was cracked, the codes were given away; SMS codes can be relayed the same way and add SIM-swap risk.

items.stem: A phishing email links to a page that was harmless when the message was delivered at 9:00, but the attacker switches it to a password-harvesting form at 11:00. Which secure email gateway feature is designed for exactly this?

choices.A: Attachment sandboxing
choices.B: DMARC enforcement
choices.C: A banner marking messages from outside the organisation
choices.D: URL rewriting that re-checks the link each time it is clicked

items.explanation: URL rewriting replaces each link with one that passes through the gateway, so the destination is evaluated at the moment of the click rather than only at delivery. A page that turned malicious after the message arrived is still caught when the user finally clicks it.

rationale.A: Sandboxing opens attachments in an isolated environment to watch their behaviour; this message carries a link, not a file.
rationale.B: DMARC decides whether the sender's domain is authentic; it never examines where a link leads, and a phishing message sent from the attacker's own properly configured domain passes it.
rationale.C: An external-sender banner is a useful cue to slow down, but it does not evaluate the link at all.

items.stem: A company runs DMARC at p=reject, a secure email gateway, and annual awareness training. A finance employee still wires millions to criminals after an email, sent from the real but taken-over mailbox of a known business partner, asks for an urgent change of bank details. Which assessment of the company's controls is most accurate?

choices.A: The email controls did what they were built to do, because the message really did come from the partner's domain; the missing layer was a process control requiring out-of-band verification of any payment change
choices.B: DMARC failed and should be relaxed from p=reject to p=quarantine so suspicious mail is kept for review
choices.C: The gateway should have blocked the message, since an email with no link or attachment is itself a sign of fraud
choices.D: The controls were complete; the fault lies only with the employee, and more frequent training would have been enough

items.explanation: Business email compromise from a genuine, compromised mailbox passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC because the mail truly originates where it claims to, and it carries no link or payload for a gateway to flag. That is why the chapter's Toyota Boshoku case calls for an organisational control on top of the technical ones: confirm any change to payment instructions by calling a number looked up independently. The loss came from a missing layer, not from a broken one.

rationale.B: The message passed authentication legitimately, so no DMARC policy would have stopped it, and quarantine is a weaker setting than reject, not a stronger one.
rationale.C: Most legitimate business email is plain text with no link or attachment; blocking on that basis would stop normal mail, and it is the absence of a technical signature that makes BEC hard to catch.
rationale.D: Training targets System 1 habits but cannot be relied on alone, especially under urgency and authority pressure; a high-value process with no verification step is an organisational gap.

items.stem: An organisation that has never published DMARC wants to stop attackers spoofing its domain. The security lead proposes publishing p=reject on day one. Why is the usual rollout to begin at p=none?

choices.A: A domain may only publish p=reject after it has been registered for a full year
choices.B: At p=none the domain receives reports on every service sending as it, so legitimate third-party senders such as payroll or newsletter platforms can be authenticated before enforcement starts refusing their mail
choices.C: p=none blocks spoofed mail more gently by adding a warning banner instead of deleting it
choices.D: p=reject would also block the mail the organisation receives from other domains

items.explanation: DMARC's "R" is reporting. Starting at p=none takes no action on failing mail but shows the domain owner every source sending in its name. Outside services that send on the company's behalf, and are not yet covered by SPF or DKIM, would otherwise be rejected the moment enforcement begins. The usual path is p=none to find them, then p=quarantine, then p=reject.

rationale.A: No such waiting period exists; a domain owner can publish any DMARC policy at any time.
rationale.C: p=none takes no action at all on failing mail; it is monitoring only, and banners are a gateway feature, not a DMARC policy.
rationale.D: A DMARC policy governs mail that claims to come from the publishing domain; it has no effect on mail the organisation receives from anyone else.

items.stem: After a vishing campaign in which callers posed as IT support and talked staff into "updating VPN settings" on a lookalike portal, a company wants layered controls that each break a different step of the attack. Which set does this best?

choices.A: Longer passwords, quarterly password changes, and a company password manager
choices.B: A stricter spam filter, DMARC at p=reject, and attachment sandboxing
choices.C: A rule that IT never asks for credentials by phone, with staff calling back on the published helpdesk number; FIDO2 keys for VPN and admin sign-in; and admin tools limited to the few people who need them
choices.D: A yearly awareness video and phishing posters in every office

items.explanation: Each layer stops a different step. The call-back rule removes the authority pretext, because staff verify through a channel they chose. FIDO2 keys mean credentials typed into the lookalike portal cannot be used on the real site. Least privilege on admin tools limits what one compromised account can reach; in the 2020 Twitter case those tools let the attackers take over high-profile accounts.

rationale.A: Password strength does not matter when the victim types the password into the attacker's page; none of these controls address the phone call or the stolen session.
rationale.B: These are email controls, and the attack arrived by phone and a web portal; none of them touch either channel.
rationale.D: Awareness alone is a single layer with no technical backstop, and one hurried employee is enough for the attack to succeed.

items.stem: A teacher gets a WhatsApp message from an unknown number showing the principal's photo: "In a meeting, can't talk. Buy five ₹2,000 gift cards for the staff prize draw and send me the codes now." Which principle of influence is the attacker mainly relying on?

choices.A: Authority
choices.B: Social proof
choices.C: Reciprocity
choices.D: Liking

items.explanation: The attacker borrows the principal's position so the teacher complies without checking: requests from a senior person are rarely questioned. Asking for gift-card codes, which can't be traced or reversed, is a classic sign of this scam.

rationale.B: Social proof points to what others are doing ("the whole staff room has paid"); the message makes no such claim.
rationale.C: Reciprocity works by giving the target something first so they feel they owe a favour; nothing is offered here.
rationale.D: Liking relies on friendliness or shared interests; this message is curt and uses rank, not rapport.

items.stem: Two vishing callers each ask an employee to read out a one-time code "to finish a mailbox upgrade". Caller 1 knows the employee's manager's name and the name of the company's IT ticket system; Caller 2 knows neither. Why is Caller 1 more likely to succeed?

choices.A: The inside details make the pretext believable, so the employee is less likely to stop and verify the request
choices.B: Knowing internal names lets the caller skip the one-time code entirely
choices.C: Employees are trained to obey anyone who can name their manager
choices.D: The details prove the caller is on the company's internal network

items.explanation: Pretexting works by building a believable story. Small true details, often gathered from LinkedIn or old emails, lower suspicion so the target skips checks such as calling IT back on a known number.

rationale.B: The details change nothing technical: the caller still needs the code, which is exactly why they ask for it.
rationale.C: Training teaches the opposite, to verify; the details exploit trust, not a rule.
rationale.D: Names can be found on social media and public posts; they prove nothing about where the caller is.

items.stem: After a phishing incident at a school in Pune, the IT lead must classify the attack for the report. Evidence: the email went only to the three staff who approve fee refunds, attached the school's real refund form, and named the parent whose refund was "overdue". Which classification is best supported?

choices.A: Spear phishing, because the message was tailored to specific people using details about their role
choices.B: Whaling, because the message targeted the school's most senior leaders
choices.C: Mass phishing, because the attacker used a real form that any school might send
choices.D: Smishing, because the attack used an attachment instead of a link

items.explanation: Spear phishing targets chosen individuals with researched details: role-specific recipients, a real form and a real parent's name. Whaling is spear phishing aimed at top executives, and these recipients were chosen for their job function, not seniority.

rationale.B: Whaling targets top leaders such as the principal or trustees; fee-refund staff were picked for their role.
rationale.C: Mass phishing is untargeted and sent widely; three recipients with role-specific bait is the opposite.
rationale.D: Smishing is phishing by SMS; this arrived by email, and attachments versus links don't define the channel.

items.stem: Staff at an office keep holding the badge-controlled door open for people carrying boxes. Which control most directly reduces this tailgating risk?

choices.A: Awareness posters about phishing emails
choices.B: A turnstile or mantrap that admits one person per badge swipe
choices.C: A sign-in sheet for visitors at reception
choices.D: CCTV recording at the entrance

items.explanation: A turnstile or mantrap physically enforces one entry per credential, so politeness at the door can no longer let a stranger in. It prevents tailgating rather than just recording it.

rationale.A: Phishing posters address email, not behaviour at a door.
rationale.C: A sign-in sheet only records visitors who choose to stop at reception; a tailgater walks straight past.
rationale.D: CCTV records the tailgater for later review but doesn't stop them getting in.

items.stem: An HR officer receives an email from an employee's personal Gmail address asking to change their salary bank account before this month's payroll run. Which control best stops payroll diversion fraud here?

choices.A: Asking the employee to confirm by replying to the same email
choices.B: Verifying the request through a known channel, such as calling the number in HR records or meeting in person, before changing details
choices.C: Checking that the email has no spelling mistakes
choices.D: Making the change but watching the new account for a month

items.explanation: Out-of-band verification breaks the attacker's control of the channel: if the email account or address is fake, a call to the number already on record reaches the real employee.

rationale.A: A reply goes back to whoever sent the email, so the attacker simply confirms their own request.
rationale.C: Fraudsters, and AI tools, write flawless emails; good spelling proves nothing.
rationale.D: By the time anyone watches the account, the salary has been paid to the attacker.

items.stem: A college's IT team has budget for one new control after callers posing as the helpdesk talked staff into approving MFA push prompts. Which option best addresses the root cause?

choices.A: An extra awareness session telling staff never to approve unexpected pushes
choices.B: Raising the minimum password length from 10 to 14 characters
choices.C: Blocking international calls to staff desk phones
choices.D: Replacing push approvals with phishing-resistant security keys (FIDO2), which can't be approved on someone else's behalf

items.explanation: The weakness was that a push could be approved for a login the user didn't start. A FIDO2 key only signs in for the person physically holding it, on the real site, so no caller can talk a victim into approving their login. Training still helps, but it isn't a technical fix.

rationale.A: Training helps, but people under pressure still get talked into it; the weakness stays in place.
rationale.B: The attackers already had the passwords; length doesn't matter once a password is known.
rationale.C: Caller ID is easily spoofed and attackers can use local numbers.
